items.question: What happens to the body and experience when the vital breath breaks apart?
premises: The vital breath can become disjoined from its normal functioning.
When the breath breaks apart, the body appears as inert matter.
A new sphere of experience arises according to the sequence of prior latent impressions.
items.inference: At the disruption of the vital breath, the body falls into inert appearance and consciousness passes into another experiential domain shaped by prior impressions.
uncertainties: The exact scope of adhikāra here, whether a new life-domain or a new experiential jurisdiction, is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: When the vital breath breaks apart, the body appears inert, and one passes into another sphere of experience that arises according to the sequence of earlier latent impressions.

rows.grounds: in that very state or domain
the condition of being like stone
experiences or cognizes; sandhi form of vetti

items.question: What kinds of experience can arise in that post-disruption state?
premises: In that same state, one may construct an experience called the other world.
Alternatively, one may experience a stone-like insentient condition.
Alternatively, one may awaken again to ordinary awareness.
items.inference: The state following the breath's disruption can manifest as an other-world experience, as inert stupor, or as a return to waking awareness.
uncertainties: Whether pāṣāṇatāṃ refers to literal insentience, deep coma, or a metaphorical rigidity is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: In that very state one may fashion an experience called the other world, or one may feel like stone, or else one may wake up again.

rows.grounds: in whatever way it has become settled

items.question: How does an experience come to count as another world or as heaven and liberation?
premises: The designation 'this is another world' depends on a subject's firm conviction.
Heaven, liberation, and similar states become established in a person's mind in specific ways.
What is firmly settled in consciousness determines how such states are taken.
items.inference: Other-world status and states like heaven or liberation are constituted by the way they become firmly established in consciousness.
uncertainties: The verse spans into the next verse for its full consequence; the syntactic completion is carried forward.
items.plain_english: It is called another world because of one's firm conviction, and whatever heaven, liberation, or the like has become settled in the mind for someone here takes shape accordingly.

rows.grounds: even in that domain; sandhi of tatra + api

items.question: What forms of experience appear outwardly as a result of settled inner conviction?
premises: What is firmly established in consciousness appears outwardly for that subject.
Even in that projected domain there is manifold variety.
Bondage, liberation, happiness, heaven, suffering, and inert states can all appear there.
items.inference: The outwardly appearing world, including its highest and lowest states, is a varied manifestation shaped by consciousness.
items.plain_english: In just that way it shines outwardly for that person, and so even there there is variety: bondage and liberation, happiness and heaven, suffering and an inert state.

items.question: What is the ultimate nature that manifests all these varied experiential states?
premises: Consciousness alone manifests independently in these ways.
This independent manifestation is of the nature of Śiva.
In a being composed of parts, the sense of 'I' abides only to a limited extent.
items.inference: The diverse appearances of experience are the free self-manifestation of consciousness whose nature is Śiva, though finite beings know this 'I' only in a limited way.
items.plain_english: Consciousness alone, in its own freedom, shines forth in this way as Śiva-nature; and just as a being made of parts has an 'I'-sense only to a limited extent,

items.question: How does Bhairava's universal I-sense relate to the way imagined objects appear real?
premises: Bhairava's I-sense abides in a form whose nature is the whole universe.
A child can perceive a goblin even in an empty place.
What is thus perceived can appear to produce real effects.
items.inference: Just as a child's cognition can make an unreal figure appear effectively real, consciousness in its universal Bhairava-form freely manifests appearances with seeming reality.
items.plain_english: so too Bhairava's 'I'-sense abides in a form that is the whole universe; just as a child, even in an empty place, perceives a goblin as something that produces real effects.
